claims.text: An integrated DFT-CALPHAD-quasi-chemical protocol can accurately and efficiently predict melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
The intended initial materials are single-phase disordered FCC or BCC HEAs near their melting temperatures.
Configurational entropy is predominant in high-temperature HEAs close to their melting points.
EMTO-CPA finite-temperature calculations can include electronic, magnetic, and phononic free-energy contributions for disordered metallic alloys.
VASP with suitable thermal and magnetic corrections can provide the required finite-temperature free energies for this HEA-wide melting protocol.
CALPHAD provides Gibbs-energy descriptions that efficiently determine composition-dependent phase stability and multicomponent phase diagrams.
Combining CALPHAD descriptions with quasi-chemical models captures liquid-phase and melting-transition properties.
The disordered local moment state controls high-temperature phase stability in the targeted HEAs.
Pronounced short-range order can cause significant deviations from ideal configurational mixing behavior.
A DLM, configurationally stabilized single-phase structure underpins the proposed predictive framework.
Combining DFT finite-temperature energy contributions with CALPHAD Gibbs-energy models yields the thermodynamic parameters governing melting.
Concentration-weighted pressure corrections and semiempirical adjustments properly handle liquid properties and volume changes at melting.
The integrated protocol will predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change within approximately 5-10% of experiment across multiple HEA compositions.
Existing computational methods used in isolation generally have errors of 10-15% or more.
Existing isolated computational methods require extensive tuning and are inefficient over wide HEA composition spaces.
The integrated approach will be less reliable for alloys with significant short-range order, local clustering, or phase segregation.
The approach is most applicable to alloys that remain highly disordered near melting.
Quantitatively capturing subtle vibrational and magnetic contributions remains uncertain in extremely compositionally complex alloys.
An average prediction error greater than 15% across the tested composition range would falsify the proposed approach.
